Strong raw accuracy is not enough—miscalibrated probabilities distort edge computation, stake sizing and CLV. If you are new to probability edges read Value Betting first, then connect sizing concepts from Bankroll Management. Expected Calibration Error (ECE): Bucket probability range (0–0.05,...,0.95–1.0) and compute weighted |avg\_pred - empirical\_freq|. Mid-range inflation (0.35–0.65 predicted > realized) => model overconfident around uncertainty region (reduces edge filter precision in Value Betting). Apply recalibration mapping after raw model prediction but before edge = (Odds \* p) - 1 computation used in Value Betting workflows. Recompute thresholds (e.g. min edge 3%) using calibrated probabilities only to avoid inflated position sizes in bankroll strategy. Accurate but miscalibrated models leak EV via mis-sized stakes and noisy edge filters—undermining the concepts in Value Betting. results.title: Decoding Model Performance Metrics: Confusion Matrix, ROC Curve, and AUC
results.content: Published Time: 2024-01-14T18:50:24-05:00 Decoding Model Performance Metrics: Confusion Matrix, ROC Curve, and AUC - Jeremy Mathew #### Jeremy Mathew ##### Jeremy Mathew ###### Python ###### R ###### SQL ###### Tableau Decoding Model Performance Metrics: Confusion Matrix, ROC Curve, and AUC Machine learning models can sometimes feel like a black box – you put data in and get predictions out. In this post, I’ll explain what these metrics mean in simple language so you can better understand model evaluation. A confusion matrix is essentially a scorecard for your machine learning model, showing how often it was right or wrong in its predictions. 2. Predicted Values: These columns show what your MODEL predicted the outcome was (like whether it predicted that the patient had the disease). By comparing the actual versus predicted values, you can easily see where your model was correctly saying “yes” or “no” versus where it got confused or made mistakes. ROC Curve: The Performance Plot An ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve shows your model’s predictive performance at ALL possible classification thresholds – not just a single cutoff point like in the confusion matrix. 1. True Positive Rate: How often the model correctly said “yes” (like correctly diagnosing patients who are sick). 2. False Positive Rate: How often the model incorrectly said “yes” (like telling healthy patients they are sick). The visual curve lets you see if your model does this consistently across various decision thresholds. A rising diagonal line means your model is no better than random guessing! Finally, the AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) boils down model performance into a single number between 0 and 1. A higher AUC signals a better model: * AUC = 0.5 means your model might as well randomly guess classes. * AUC = 1 means your model has perfect predictive accuracy. So in summary, use the confusion matrix to audit the correctness of predictions, visualize the ROC curve to see performance consistency, and simplify into an AUC number to benchmark against other models! Evaluating machine learning models isn’t so confusing after all. I hope this post helped explain these common model evaluation metrics intuitively!
